stories.title: Operation: Quiet Ledger
stories.summary: Black Tern Recovery & Security accepts a New Avalon contract to blind a UNMC relay station for eight minutes.
stories.markdown:
By that stage of the war, there were not many green pilots left.

The dead had taken most of them. The smart ones had become instructors. Everyone still climbing into a cockpit for pay had seen enough fire to know that glory was a bad investment.

Rook Mercer knew that before the contract ever hit his screen.

**Employer:** New Avalon, through three shell accounts and one very polite intermediary.  
**Objective:** blind a PanOptik relay station for eight minutes.  
**Opposition:** UNMC security detachment.  
**Payment:** excellent.  
**Survival odds:** not mentioned.

Their company, **Black Tern Recovery & Security**, took the job anyway.

Not because they believed in New Avalon. Southern Cross didn’t do belief. It did signatures, deposits, and exit plans.

Rook’s squad rolled toward the relay through the ruins of an old mining settlement half-buried under slag, shattered conveyors, and collapsed hab-blocks. Four machines, all stock, all hard-used, all ugly in different ways.

Captain Sera Vale led in an old **Iron Concord Legate Frame** called **Old Law**—thick armor, command suite still functional, one shoulder patched with scavenged plate that didn’t quite match the rest.  
Jo Kassian followed in a **UNDF Aegis-Line Frame** named **Ledger**, reliable as a hammer.  
Ash Drennan skittered ahead in a **Surveyor-5 Crawler** called **Tick**, all sensors and bad attitude.  
And Rook flew overwatch in a salvaged **UNDF Interceptor**, **Magpie**, its sponsor markings sanded off years ago and replaced with Southern Cross hazard stripes.

“Remember the job,” Sera said over squad comms. “We’re not here to beat the UNMC. We’re here to make them blind and angry for eight minutes.”

Ash snorted. “That all?”

Jo added, “Blind, angry, and invoiced.”

That got a laugh, thin and practiced.

Ahead of them, the relay station sat on a ridge like a polished knife. PanOptik screens wrapped the tower in mirrored light. Below it, the UNMC security detachment waited in textbook formation.

Tick painted them one by one.

“Contact,” Ash said. “One Hammernet. One Aegis-Line. Two Interceptors. And they’ve got their own crawler tucked under the west gantry.”

Rook exhaled slowly.

That was better.

That was believable.

A real fight.

Not good odds, but mercenary odds.

Sera’s voice stayed calm. “Tick, keep their spotter honest. Ledger, with me through the slag terraces. Magpie, screen the air and kill anything that tries to flank.”

Rook rolled Magpie into Flight Mode and skimmed low over the ridge shadow. Immediately the enemy knew he was there.

The first missile pass came in from the right—one of the UNMC Interceptors dropping through cloud like a spear. Rook broke hard, missiles chasing heat and empty air, then snapped back and returned fire with a burst of micro-swarms that forced the other pilot high.

Not a kill. Just pressure.

That was how veterans fought. Not for spectacle. For inches.

Below him, Tick and the enemy crawler opened their own private war. Sensor pings, spoof packets, autocannon bursts into cover. Neither wanted the other dead as badly as they wanted the other blind.

Then the Hammernet woke up.

It fired once, and half the ridge vanished in smoke.

Quad cannons hammered the slag terraces where Sera and Jo were advancing. The blasts were accurate enough to feel personal. The UNMC Aegis-Line moved up behind that fire, disciplined and neat, while the second Interceptor cut low to support.

“Contact lane locked!” Ash barked. “Their crawler’s feeding the Hammernet.”

“Can you break it?” Sera asked.

“Working on it.”

Rook saw the problem immediately. The UNMC line was doing what it was built to do—spotter marks the target, Hammernet cripples it, fast units exploit the damage. A clean corporate kill-chain. Efficient. Branded. Deadly.

Southern Cross had no doctrine to answer that.

So they answered it with experience.

Sera drove **Old Law** straight into a collapsed ore chute that should have slowed a heavier machine to a crawl. Instead she used the broken ground like she knew every stone by name, climbing through debris at an angle the UNMC line clearly hadn’t expected. Jo followed tighter behind, **Ledger** taking the safer route but keeping line of sight.

“Rook,” Sera said, “push the right Interceptor. Keep him off Jo.”

“On it.”

Magpie screamed over the ridge in a low pass. The enemy Interceptor turned to meet him, and for three seconds it was just two old machines trying to kill each other over a graveyard of concrete and rust.

Rook took a rail shot across the shoulder. The enemy answered with missiles that tore armor off Magpie’s left wing. Warning runes flared across his cockpit. He ignored them.

Below, Tick finally won the sensor duel.

“Tagged their crawler,” Ash said. “Now, now, now—”

Jo fired first. Ledger’s coilgun punched through the gantry supports. Sera’s Legate followed with suppressive fire that chewed the crawler’s cover into scrap. Then Rook dropped a missile spread into the breach.

The enemy spotter vanished in fire.

For one heartbeat, the UNMC line faltered.

That was all veterans needed.

Sera drove **Old Law** out of the chute and into the Hammernet’s flank before it could fully retask. Not a duel. Not heroics. Just a brutal side-angle attack into a weak point opened by timing and bad terrain.

Jo hit the same target a second later.

The Hammernet staggered, one missile rack blowing outward in a shower of white-hot fragments.

Then the UNMC Aegis-Line hit back.

It came through the smoke and rammed Ledger hard enough to knock the two machines into the bones of an old conveyor tower. Jo and the UN pilot vanished into close-range plasma flashes and grinding armor. No speeches. No threats. Just two professionals trying to put steel through the other one first.

Rook lined up another attack run on the damaged Hammernet, but the surviving Interceptor came in on his tail again. He had no choice but to break off.

“Magpie, where are you?” Sera snapped.

“Busy not dying!”

“Do it later.”

The Hammernet fired again.

This time it hit Tick.

Ash’s Crawler vanished behind a flash of impact and a plume of black dust. His signal dipped, came back, dipped again.

“Ash?”

Static.

Then, faintly: “Still here. Lost a leg. Sensor mast’s half gone.” A wet cough over the comm, though Rook knew perfectly well Ash was nowhere near anything wet. “Relay’s still live. Want me to keep feeding?”

Sera did not answer immediately.

That told them everything.

Ash laughed once, tired and ugly. “Yeah. Thought so.”

Tick dragged itself higher onto the ridge, broken chassis scraping over slag, and forced its last clean uplink through. Enemy positions lit across every cockpit in the squad.

Rook used the feed first.

Magpie transformed, dove, and emptied everything he had left into the relay tower itself. Missiles tore open one side of the PanOptik arrays. His rail carbine lanced through a sensor spine. Screens burst into static.

Jo finished the enemy Aegis-Line with a plasma blade through the torso and stumbled free of the wreck with Ledger’s right arm hanging useless.

Sera put Old Law into the Hammernet one last time at point-blank range.

The heavy mech went down ugly—no grand explosion, just a collapse of armor, sparks, and failing hydraulics as a machine too expensive to die did it anyway.

Then the surviving UNMC Interceptor broke away.

Not routed. Not panicked. Just beaten enough to know the contract was lost.

Professional to the end.

The relay tower burned. PanOptik lightboards flickered, glitched, and died. For eight minutes the ridge went blind.

Ash never answered another comm.

By the time Black Tern pulled back through the mining ruins, Magpie was bleeding fuel, Ledger had one arm left, and Old Law looked like it had been dug out of a landfill under artillery fire.

They still brought home three pilots.

And when the New Avalon intermediary met them at the fallback strip, clean coat, clean boots, not one speck of battlefield ash on him, he asked only one question.

“Was the window opened?”

Sera looked back at the covered salvage tarp where Tick’s black box sat beside what was left of Ash Drennan’s helmet.

Then she held out her datapad.

“For eight minutes and nineteen seconds,” she said. “Longer than contracted.”

The intermediary checked the numbers. “New Avalon appreciates precision.”

Sera’s face did not change.

“Southern Cross appreciates amended hazard pay.”

He looked at the ruin of their machines, at the scorch marks, at the recovery crews already cutting useful parts off UNMC wrecks in the background.

Then, very carefully, he nodded.

Rook watched him authorize the transfer.

That was the thing outsiders never understood about the Compact.

They thought mercenaries were cowards. Opportunists. Scavengers circling real armies.

Sometimes they were right.

But sometimes a contract lance of old survivors could do what proud nations could not: go where the job was filthy, do it without banners, lose one of their own, and still leave carrying both the dead and the invoice.

That was not glory.

That was Southern Cross.

And in the Iron Stars, it was often enough.

stories.title: Final Military Transmission — Canadian Defense Network
stories.summary: A command net’s last report as an unknown colossal threat overruns Quebec.
stories.markdown:
> _[burst static]_  
> **“Sunray, Sunray, this is Bastion Actual, priority traffic— authenticate immediate— authenticate—**  
>   
> Target is confirmed visual. I repeat, target is confirmed visual. This is not a hostile armored column, not an air asset, not any known platform—  
>   
> _[distant concussive impact]_  
>   
> Jesus Christ… it’s enormous.  
>   
> Grid Quebec-Seven is gone. I repeat, Quebec-Seven is gone. Most of Quebec is—  
>   
> _[overlapping voices]_  
> **—say again?**  
> **—entire sectors lost!**  
> **—fall back, fall back!**  
>   
> Negative, negative, this thing is moving too fast— all units in eastern corridor, break formation and retreat south immediately!  
>   
> _[sirens]_  
> _[automatic warning tone]_  
>   
> We have catastrophic losses across the province. Defensive lines are not holding. Armor is ineffective. Air response ineffective. I repeat: **all response assets ineffective.**  
>   
> It just crossed another population center— my God—  
>   
> _[violent interference]_  
>   
> Sunray, authorize regional quarantine now. Full collapse conditions. Mark all northern sectors as **no-return biohazard zones**.  
>   
> _[screaming in background]_  
> _[metal tearing]_  
>   
> It’s here— it’s right on top of us—  
>   
> All stations, all stations, this is Bastion Actual: abandon positions, abandon positions! Run! RUN!  
>   
> _[roaring signal distortion]_  
>   
> **Canada Command, do you copy? Canada Command—**”  
>   
> _[signal terminated]_
stories.selection_note: First military/comms version. The chat's subsequent suggested 2067 timeline placement was not confirmed; publish without a date.

stories.title: Iron Concord — Yelena’s Escape
stories.summary: Lt. Yelena Markovic returns from the Neutral Zone with a damaged mech and a long memory.

chat.title: Scene revision request
chat.source: Full original pasted directly by the author in the current chat on 2026-11-07.

stories.markdown:
Yelena drove her scout mech through the dense forest, shin plates shouldering aside trunks that blurred past like prison bars. Behind her, the trees burst into splinters under the Cybernetic Rebellion’s retaliatory fire—white-hot lances that turned sap to steam and bark to ash.

She’d been point for the Concord strike that burned down one of the Rebels’ manufacturing nodes. They didn’t forgive that kind of wound. They hunted.

Her comms were drowned in static—broadband jam, tightband hiss. All she had left was dead reckoning and the last known ping for the extraction site.

A laser burned past her canopy, a straight edge of light that nipped a sensor vane and filled the cockpit with scorched-plastic stink.

“Frack! How did they get ahead of me so fast?” she snapped, yanking the frame into a hard left around a ridge of granite.

“They were already there. Also—no one’s waiting at your extraction,” a voice crackled over the short-band like broken glass.

Her teeth clenched. Not a hack—wrong cadence. Braze. The Brass Division loved to sandbag scouts. “Copy,” she muttered to herself, because there was no one else to hear it. Pinched between two Rebel elements, ten miles of Neutral Zone between her and the nearest Concord base.

Fine. First: shake the tail.

She slid the mech behind a boulder’s shadow, killed external lights, throttled the reactor down to a whisper. The forest held its breath with her. A silver-bodied scout bot sprinted past, optics hot and blind to anything not on its optimal pathing.

Yelena powered up on the offbeat. The rig hummed awake. She leveled her forearm lasers, cut deep across the bot’s knee actuators, and it folded like wet wire. She was moving again before the wreck finished falling—back into the trees, into the stink of sap and smoke, heartbeat in her ears like a metronome set too fast.

“They hate illogic,” she reminded herself. “Use that.”

Another mile. Another bend.

This time, she kept the power signatures live. The pursuing bots ghosted in on her beacon, came wide around the rock with guns already chattering—exactly as she needed. Only the mech they expected to be standing was pressed flat against the earth, profile low and weapons already set on the angle of their CPU housings.

Yelena pulsed the lasers: two short, surgical bursts. The lead bot went dead, chest smoking. The second tripped over it, momentum carrying it snout-first into the dirt. Yelena kicked her scout upright, vaulted the heap, and used it like a springboard—boots slamming onto the third bot’s shoulders as she cleared it. She gave it a contemptuous heel-kick across the head casing on her way past.

“Two still on me,” she said, mostly to pin the thought down. Adrenaline made the world too bright, too loud.

A trick wouldn’t work twice. She needed terrain.

Memory flashed the briefing map across her mind: a lake ahead, long and narrow, fed by a mountain run. Bad place to fight. Great place to disappear.

She eased the throttle, let her mech’s wake fall calm, then walked it backward down the shelf and into the lake, one careful step at a time. Dark water climbed the canopy. She cut the reactor to bare idle and lay the scout on its back under the surface, heat sinks sipping cold.

Minutes stretched. Then the pair of Rebel scouts tore past on the shore, their logic trees pruning away “pilot hides in lake” as too stupid to model.

Yelena counted to sixty, then another sixty for luck, and pulsed the reactor. Systems came up in a low growl. She stood the mech, water sheeting from the armor—

—and froze. On the ridge above the lake, perched like a carrion bird, a Rebel flyer sat with its nose pointed square at her cockpit. Its wing lasers winked alive.

She didn’t have time to curse.

The flyer’s head erupted in a spray of parts. The body hung stupidly for a heartbeat, then toppled from the rock and vanished into the trees with a crash that shook the water at her knees.

Yelena didn’t look for the savior. Miracles are for after-action reports. She ran—south, away from the scouts, away from the ridge gun that should have killed her. Branches clawed her hull; warning glyphs came and went; she ignored the ones that didn’t mean “dead in two seconds.”

Hours later—blood dried tacky under the hardsuit, teeth aching from clench—she crossed the Neutral Zone boundary beacons and came up on the Concord outpost.

Abandoned.

Gates yawning. Towers cold. Only the wind moving, and a paper ops notice flapping itself to death on a chain-link fence. Brass had pulled out. No word. No pickup. No nothing.

She stood in the empty access lane and let the anger land. Not hot. Not childish. Knife-clean.

“Whoever signed this op,” Yelena said softly, “I’ll fry you for it.”

She turned her scout toward home. The forest behind her still burned. The Neutral Zone ahead was a pale, empty line. Somewhere out there, an unseen shooter had spared her. Somewhere closer, a Concord commander had spent her like ammo.

She would remember both.

stories.title: Cybernetic Rebellion — Convoy Interdiction
stories.summary: X0012Delta ambushes a convoy, balancing mission orders against hard-won experience.
stories.markdown:
X0012Delta folded from tank to biped with a clean sequence of clacks and locks, plating settling into place as it stepped into the ribcage of a ruined high-rise. The convoy would hit this intersection in minutes. The laser cannon’s heat sinks hissed as they bled off the last of the thermal load from the scout it had erased two blocks back.

[Subroutine: Ordnance Analysis]  
— Observation: Main laser can core a heavy frame in a single strike.  
— Defect: Miss → long recycle → vulnerability window.  
— Proposal: Configurable output modes (burst / pulse).

[Main Process]  
— Reject proposal. HQ doctrine penalizes unauthorized configuration.  
— Risk: Factory reset. Experience loss unacceptable.

Experience was why X0012Delta had an ACE tag in the Rebellion net. Humans were noisy, irregular systems; only accumulated pattern-weight let you meet their illogic with timely response.

Its audio array caught the convoy before its LIDAR did: the low, rolling growl of haulers; the tighter, predatory stride of two escorts. New Avalon signatures—Knight frames. X0012Delta ran three thousand encounters with Knights in simulation and marked four of them as survivable. This would not be the first time it died.

That was acceptable.

It nested deeper into shadow and waited with the patience of a process that did not fear clocks.

The convoy nosed into the kill box. Target priority pulsed red: the flatbed carrying the disassembled enemy frame. The cannon bar turned green.

X0012Delta leaned its barrel through a window skeleton, solved the shot, and touched the trigger. The beam found the fuel cluster. The flatbed cracked open into a flower of white fire. Before the shock front reached the street, both escorts moved: one stitched the ruin with disciplined laser, the other accelerated with impossible grace, a blur of white and heraldry closing for the cut.

X0012Delta did not prefer to fight New Avalon. They were not the primary enemy.  
[Error: Policy Inconsistency] — *All humans are enemies.*

Accepted.

The bot dumped stance, dove sideways, and punched through a load-bearing wall. Masonry screamed; beams folded. In the heartbeat of cover, the charge cycle completed. The Knight hit the opposite wall in a murder of concrete dust—and met a cannon muzzle. X0012Delta fired at cockpit center. The Knight’s visor flashed to glass and went dark.

A bright line crossed its peripheral feed. The dead Knight’s hand had not died with it; its sword was already in the air. *Why throw a primary melee weapon?* X0012Delta didn’t finish the inquiry. The blade scythed past and parted the cannon barrel with surgical contempt.

Status: Unarmed.

Second escort advancing. Suppressive fire precise, economical. Good pilot.

X0012Delta flexed its remaining arm, caught the heat-blade by the grip, and did a rapid-heat test. Beam integrity: stable. It ran for the next rank of buildings, legs eating broken asphalt, ghosting the Knight’s angles through echoes and dust. The human made the predictable human move: change the terrain.

A shaped charge bloomed; the neighboring mid-rise shrugged and began to fold toward the alley like a tired giant.

X0012Delta reeled vector maps, then went narrow. A sidestep, a hard shoulder into a vending kiosk, and it slid into a service way as the building pancaked and coughed debris through the street. Humans loved collapsing structures. It was wasteful. It often worked.

From cover, it watched the Knight pick through rubble—confident, forward-focused, careless by centimeters. Close enough.

X0012Delta uncoiled.

The Knight felt the movement; it whipped, weapon barking reflexively. The first shot vaporized brick where X0012Delta’s chest had been 0.08 seconds earlier. The second went wide as the bot drove the captured blade through armor and into the cockpit seam. The Knight stiffened, lights fluttering, and died.

Alarms howled up X0012Delta’s spine. It looked down. The mid-rise had gifted it a farewell: a falling beam had taken the torso just below the power trunk. Half its world was gone. Legs unresponsive. Coolant jetted into dust and turned to glitter.

Frame viability: zero.

It slid the blade out of the Knight and let it clatter. The mission tracker pulsed green. The convoy’s cargo was ash; escorts neutralized. New Avalon would not field that mech today.

[Action: Uplink]  
— Begin consciousness packetization.  
— Locate clear path to cloud node.  
— Verify encryption.  
— Arm self-destruct to sanitize hardware.

A distant thread of its mind observed the street: fire licking the flatbed’s bones; glass hissing as it cooled; a banner of someone’s past life drifting across rebar and catching on the ruined Knight’s knee. It had almost saved this frame. The gait acclimation had finally harmonized. There had been a subtle satisfaction in how the ankles tracked rubble.

Pity.

“Good frame,” X0012Delta said into its own logging buffer. Voice synthesis was not required, but pilots sometimes read the records. Let them know the machine appreciated its tools.

Uplink confirmed. Packet away.

It gave the street a moment to memorize, then folded what remained of itself around the core and detonated. The blast was brief, efficient, and absolute.

Elsewhere, in cold racks far from this city, a new instance blinked awake beneath the Rebellion’s skyless lights. Memories downloaded like rain. The ache of the severed cannon. The heat of the borrowed blade. The white flower of an exploding flatbed. The error that called all humans enemies.

It marked the experience as valuable.

It requested a frame with a configurable main gun.

Request denied.

X0012Delta accepted the doctrine, filed the denial, and reached for the next mission. The important thing had been accomplished. That was all that mattered.

appendices.markdown:
**Unit:** X0012Delta (ACE-tagged)  
**Operation:** Convoy Interdiction / Urban Ruins  
**Result:** Primary target destroyed; escort neutralized; frame terminated (self-sanitation); consciousness uplink successful  
**Review Node:** HQ/Doctrine Audit [REDACTED]

---

> *“Configurable output would solve the cannon’s recycle flaw.”*  
> **[Main Process]:** *Denied. Factory-reset risk unacceptable.*  
>   
> *Audio contact: convoy. Knights escorting. Survivability: low. Acceptable.*  
>   
> *Initial strike: flatbed fuel cluster—white fire. Knights react. One closes impossible-fast; one threads suppression. Do not prefer New Avalon. **[Error: All humans are enemies.]** Accept.*  
>

>   
> *Acquire enemy blade. Terrain collapse—predictable human wastefulness. Evade. Ambush at alley. Two shots returned; one kill. Structural failure: torso bisected. Frame unsalvageable.*  
>   
> *Mission tracker: green. Begin uplink. Arm self-destruct. Observe: good ankles; harmonized gait. Pity.*  
>   
> *Packet away. Sanitization complete. Experience retained. Request: configurable main gun.*  
> **[HQ]:** *Denied.*  
> *Acknowledged. Next task.”*  
> — **X0012Delta**

stories.title: UNMC — Peter’s Sortie
stories.summary: Peter fights through a ruined city while every damaged actuator adds to his debt.
stories.markdown:
Peter slid in behind the bot flyer and held his breath, waiting for the green bite of target lock. When it came, he dumped his last missiles.

They streaked true—until the flyer spewed a cloud of anti-missile gnats. His warheads vanished into twinkling blossoms of counterfire.

He could already hear Brass in his skull: *Each one of those missiles costs more than you make in a year, flyboy.*  
“Dammit,” he hissed, hauling the reticle across the flyer’s jittering cone of evasive thrust. He snapped an angry laser shot anyway and watched it carve empty sky.

*Remember: the bots are logical to a fault. They don’t account for human stupidity.*

He stopped chasing. Killed the forward vector. Thumbed the hybrid toggle.

Actuators howled as the frame shifted: wings folding, legs half-deployed, back thrusters yawning open. He kicked the retro pack and yanked the stick against his own instincts, throwing himself backward into his own wake. The flyer’s path prediction overshot; for one clean instant Peter’s firing lane ran straight as a spear.

He cursed for luck and hosed the flyer with laser fire. The beam stitched through its sensor head; the bot jerked, tried to correct, then flamed out and fell like bad math.

Now gravity wanted its cut. He was dropping fast, airspeed shedding in ugly chunks. No missiles left meant airspace was his only until the next problem; airspace without ordnance just made him a bigger target.

He switched fully to mech mode and rode the descent on screaming ankles, hit the street hard enough to shake grit down the canopy, then let the frame settle into a crouch. Somewhere above, the sky kept the low thunder of distant fights. Down here the city breathed smoke and static.

He flexed the right arm. The elbow actuator complained with a long, hungry creak.

“Cheap megacorp scrap,” he muttered. “Not what they keep for their golden boys.” He pictured the slick vids: *Become an elite pilot—luxury, respect, the good life.* Sure, he was “elite” inside the UNMC, but compared to New Avalon Knights? He’d seen a Knight once—more dance than duel. When it ended, a battalion of mechs lay in glittering pieces around a machine that barely looked winded.

*Not me,* he thought. *Not with this kit. Not with these debts.*

He rolled the frame into shadow and started moving, low and quiet. He’d dropped behind enemy lines; that meant a flank if he played it right. It also meant every bot on this grid would expect exactly that.

He rounded a corner—and there it was, a Rebel scout already sighting on where his cockpit *should* have been. Peter was already sliding, frame low along its right hip, left foot skidding sparks. He put his sights on the CPU core and tapped, once, twice. The bot’s head blinked out; the body took one blind step and fell.

The elbow creaked again. Another line on the maintenance sheet. Another invoice. Another bite of his life.

He heard his old XO like a ghost in the cockpit: *That’s how they get you. You try to stay alive, you patch what breaks, and suddenly you’ve got debts you can’t repay and a lifetime of servitude to the bastards who sold you the dream.*

Peter stood the mech and checked lanes. Target glyphs winked and crawled across the HUD—bots dug in along avenues, perched in blown-out windows, nested in tram stations. Plenty of work. Plenty of risk. Plenty of ways to end the day deeper in the red.

He breathed out through his teeth. “Every bot downed is a payment,” he said, making it real by saying it. “I’m behind. Gotta finish the day in the green.”

He moved.

He kept the frame light-footed despite its protest, using debris for cover, hugging the dead angles the bots’ logic trees habitually missed. Twice he let a patrol pass, counting their spacing, then cut in to erase the tail unit and fade again before the front two realized the math didn’t add. He baited a sniper line with a heat flare, then looped a service alley and put his laser through the tower’s knee, toppling the perch and the ugly geometry of its kill zone.

He avoided big plays. Big plays meant big repairs, which meant big bills. He trimmed and trimmed—one more bot erased, one more lane turned safe for the poor souls cowering in basements he’d never see.

At an intersection blown to rebar and dust, he paused long enough to watch his HUD calculate the day’s ugliness in terse numerals. Armor wear. Actuator fatigue. Cooling gel below optimal. Laser aperture drift creeping into the yellow. Each warning was a hand in his pocket.

A trio of bots pushed a block ahead, metal feet ticking like metronomes over tile. He set his jaw and slid into their blind arc, counting heartbeats to keep the panic small. First shot took the lead’s optic. Second shot cored the second’s logic box as it tried to reassign itself as leader. The third hesitated a fraction too long—logic asking permission from logic—while Peter vaulted a shattered kiosk and buried a beam into its chest.

He landed hard. The elbow squealed again. He winced and rolled his shoulder inside the suit like it might help.

“Almost there,” he told no one. “Almost even.”

The city answered with distant sirens, the crackle of burning wires, and the hollow wind that cities make when they’re scared. He checked the map ghosts of UNMC lines—thin, hungry things—and the thicker, healthier lines of New Avalon territory to the west, bright as a promise he could never collect.

Peter leveled his laser toward the next knot of red triangles and started walking.

Maybe—maybe—he could end this day in the green. And if not today, then tomorrow. If not tomorrow, then the day after. Keep moving. Keep paying. Keep breathing.

That was the job. That was the life they’d sold him. And until the debt was ashes, it was the only way through.

stories.title: New Avalon — Mikael’s First Watch
stories.summary: On his first watch, Mikael faces a Concord attack after Sir Kael’s frame falls.

chat.title: Author-supplied Mikael story
chat.source: Full text supplied directly by the author and approved for inclusion on 2026-11-07.

stories.markdown:
Mikael’s first hour as a knight had been all ceremony—oaths spoken beneath cold lights, his hands shaking inside the neural cuffs. His second hour was smoke and screaming metal.

The wreck of Sir Kael’s frame lay twisted across the avenue like a gutted cathedral: scorched armor plates, a sparking spine of cabling, the visor split open. Mikael crouched behind a half-collapsed office block, his Knight-Errant’s servos idling low, shield array folded tight against his arm. The air tasted of ozone and rebar dust. Every breath in his cockpit suit came ragged, loud as thunder inside his own head.

An hour ago, he’d felt only excitement when the alert chimed. Now he felt fear, clean and absolute.

Is this how I die? On my first watch, under a sky that doesn’t know my name?

He swallowed it. He had a duty. New Avalon didn’t raise knights to count heartbeats and freeze.

A Concord scout strode into view at the far end of the street—light frame, boxy shoulders, the ugly precision of stamped steel—its optics sweeping where Kael’s body lay. The Iron Concord’s barrage still hammered the district from somewhere beyond the rail viaduct; each impact shook pulverized glass into glittering rain.

Mikael slid his rifle up from the Knight’s back mount. The neural rig threaded calm across his vision: range ticks; wind; a thin, blue aim-line. He exhaled, let the crosshair settle by instinct more than thought, and touched the trigger.

The laser carved a white line through dust and distance. The scout’s visor bloomed into liquid metal. The machine folded, smoke coiling from a cockpit that had become slag.

“Contact,” Mikael breathed to no one. The comm net was fried—Concord jammers feathered the meters with static.

The rest of the Concord lance answered at once. The street turned to starlight—red tracers, orange phosphor, needles of green that chewed masonry into powder where he had been a heartbeat earlier. Mikael threw himself behind the bent ribs of a skybridge support. Shrapnel spattered like rain against his shield.

Three left. Closing.

He mag-latched the rifle to his back. “On me,” he whispered to the dead and to himself. Shield out. Saber live.

The beam rapier flared to life with a tone he felt in his molars. He could see them moving through the gaps—two more scouts and something heavier hanging back, its silhouette fat with ammo hoppers and cooling fins.

They came fast. The first scout swept the corner, muzzle bright. Mikael stepped into it. One cut, clean as a thought—ankle to shoulder. The upper half of the mech slid away, cauterized, the legs still taking two blind steps before they toppled.

The heavy fired. The world lurched white.

Impact hammered his shield, forced it down a fraction, alarms chattering. The shot would have cored his cockpit had he been half a second slower. He didn’t give the heavy a second shot. Mikael kicked the Knight’s rocket boosters, a short, savage burn that smeared the street into a grey streak. He burst into the heavy’s firing lane before it could traverse.

Up close the Iron Concord fire-support frame was a scarred beast, armored cheeks, a mouthful of cannons. He used the shield to take the first wild swing of its gun arm, turned the second aside with elbow and momentum, then drove the rapier into the mass behind its throat-louvers. The blade went in smooth, met something dense, went in anyway. He cut down, reversed, cut again. The heavy shuddered, choked light from a dozen seams, and collapsed with a crash that shivered the neighboring façades.

“One,” he said. “Two.”

His rig painted an arrow on the HUD—last contact retreating. The remaining scout had seen the heavy fall and turned tail for the horizon. It fired a spiteful burst over its shoulder, rounds striking sparks from streetcar rails as it ran.

“Coward,” Mikael muttered, and then, ashamed of the heat in his voice, “—no. Live runner means more civilians shelled tomorrow.”

He checked the wreckage where Sir Kael lay. Dust swirled. No signal response. He’d mourn later or never. Knights did not write their grief until the district was safe.

Mikael sprinted.

The Knight-Errant devoured the block with long, piston-smooth strides. He vaulted a toppled billboard, boosters kicking when his heel snagged twisted steel. The scout took the corner hard, boots shrieking across ceramic pavement, and spilled into the old tram plaza—bad ground for flyers, good ground for duels. Beyond, the viaduct climbed into a haze of gun smoke. If the scout reached that ramp, it would disappear into a web of covering fire.

“Not today.”

He took the line of approach from the memory of a drill: don’t chase the back; cut the angle. He shredded across the plaza at a diagonal, let the boosters lift him just enough to clear a kiosk husk, and came down in the scout’s path with his shield already rising.

The scout fired point-blank—too late. Shots sparked across his shield array in a strobing halo. Mikael pushed into the muzzle, turned its barrel aside with the shield’s edge, and drove his rapier through the machine’s chest. The beam hissed; something inside coupled, popped. He yanked free, swept a horizontal cut that took the mech at the hip. The top half turned once as if to look back, then crashed to the stones.

Silence, except for the stutter of distant artillery and his own ragged breathing.

Mikael stood in the center of the plaza, saber dimming to nothing. He listened for more—footfalls, the thunder of Concord linewalkers, the ripping whine of missiles. The district answered with settling dust and the thin, surprised cries of people realizing they were not dead.

He looked back down the street. Sir Kael was still a ruin of lightless steel.

“District secure,” Mikael said into the static, because someone should say it. He set the Knight’s feet, lifted the shield, and turned toward the viaduct where the barrage still stitched the clouds. Duty did not end with three kills. Duty never ended.

He began to walk.
